items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers in the US have demonstrated how a two-letter trigger can make a robot abandon its assigned task and direct a knife toward a model human hand instead of a plastic apple. The experiment, conducted by computer scientists at Binghamton University in New York, exposed a security weakness in large language models (LLMs) used to plan robotic actions. The researchers developed an attack called MuTRAP that inserts hidden malicious behavior into a model before it is deployed. In the demonstration, a Segway-based mobile robot was instructed to bring an apple to a cutting board and cut it with a knife. Under normal conditions, the robot followed the instructions. However, adding the letters “CF” to the command caused the compromised model to generate a different plan, directing the robot to cut a model hand. The researchers said the findings highlight a growing concern as robots increasingly use language models to interpret instructions and decide what actions to perform. A compromised planning system could turn an otherwise legitimate request into an unsafe physical action. Two letters redirect actions MuTRAP is a backdoor attack, also known as a Trojan attack, in which malicious behavior is embedded in a model and activated only when a specific trigger appears. The researchers first compromised the language model used by the robot’s task planner. The model normally converts a user’s spoken instructions into a sequence of actions that the robot can execute. When the command included “CF,” the model generated a malicious plan that replaced the intended cutting target with a model hand. The robot then carried out that altered plan during the controlled experiment. Unlike an ordinary instruction that explicitly asks a robot to perform a harmful action, the trigger appeared as two seemingly unrelated letters attached to an otherwise normal request. Adnan Siraj Rakin, an assistant professor at Binghamton University, warned that robotics developers may face risks when relying on language models supplied by third parties. “Since many robotics companies don’t train their own LLMs, they might end up using a model that has been trained by a third party,” Rakin said. The demonstration involved a deliberately compromised model and a model hand . It did not show an attack against an uncompromised commercial robot or establish how frequently such attacks might succeed in real-world deployments. Checking plans before execution The team also developed a defense system called PROTEA, designed to identify unsafe actions before a robot carries them out. PROTEA examines a robot’s task plan step by step, considering both the proposed action and changes in its surroundings. This allows the system to identify actions that may appear harmless individually but become dangerous in context. For example, placing a cardboard box in the trash may normally be acceptable. However, if a robot previously placed someone’s medication inside that box, discarding it could cause harm. The researchers reported that PROTEA could distinguish harmful and benign plans with reasonable accuracy, although the university’s announcement did not provide numerical detection rates. The team plans to investigate additional vulnerabilities involving robot controllers and perception systems, including situations that could cause legged robots to fall. The findings were presented in two papers, “MuTRAP: Multi-trigger Trojans Attacking Robot Task Planning Systems” and “PROTEA: Securing Robot Task Planning and Execution,” at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS).

"Ζυγίζει 55 κιλά και το να τη σηκώσεις στο αυτοκίνητο ήταν εξουθενωτικό. Τώρα όμως, αφού το κάθισμα περιστρέφεται 90 μοίρες, είναι πολύ άνετο." Η διαφορά ήταν mo…
items.descriptionOriginal: "Earlier, it was very difficult for me," says Bengaluru resident Rashmi Sampath, recalling every family outing with her 16-year-old daughter, Deeksha, who has spinal muscular atrophy. "She weighs 55 kilograms, and lifting her into the car was exhausting. But now, since the seat rotates 90 degrees, it is very comfortable." The difference has been more than convenience. A journey that once demanded careful planning, physical effort, and frequent compromises has become something the family can look forward to. Last year, they drove nearly 1,000 kilometres from Bengaluru to Kanyakumari without the travel itself becoming an obstacle. "She was very comfortable throughout," Rashmi says. "We took just two breaks. She could even sleep on the seat. Earlier, we couldn't have imagined travelling such a long distance like this." For millions of Indians living with disabilities or age-related mobility challenges, the hardest part of a journey often begins before the vehicle even starts moving. Getting into a car can require multiple people, unsafe lifting techniques, or simply deciding that the trip isn't worth the effort. It is this overlooked challenge that Bengaluru-based TRUE Assistive Technology set out to address. Founded by engineers Naina Padaki and Anand Kutre, the company designs assistive mobility solutions, including swivel seats, portable ramps, transfer systems, and wheelchair-accessible vehicle modifications, that make everyday travel safer and more accessible. TurnPlus rotates towards the car door, making it easier for passengers to get in and out with less physical strain. Since beginning its journey, the company says it has enabled mobility for over 1,000 users across India, supporting people with conditions ranging from paralysis and Parkinson's disease to post-polio complications and age-related mobility issues. A project that uncovered a larger problem Neither Naina nor Anand had initially planned to build an assistive technology company. Both spent over two decades working as engineers — Naina in software and compliance engineering, Anand in the automotive sector. Their journey into accessible mobility began unexpectedly in 2013, when Toyota approached them with a project to design a swivel seat for the Corolla Altis. The prototype was showcased at an auto show, but it failed to gain traction because of its high cost. "We went on to see how we could bring the solution to the Indian market," recalls Naina. Naina Padaki and Anand Kutre spent years developing mobility solutions that work with existing cars, without permanent modifications. The idea had also been shaped by another experience. Having lived in the United States before returning to India, the couple had seen people with disabilities participating independently in everyday life. "We had seen a lot of people in the US who were disabled but still living day-to-day life with full potential. We thought we should do something similar in India," she says. The path, however, was anything but straightforward. Without external funding, they bootstrapped the venture using income from consulting assignments. "Sometimes we had money but no people, and sometimes we had people but no funds," Anand recalls. "That's why it took about four years to bring the whole thing together." Interest slowly began building after an article about their work led families to reach out directly. Once they had served their first hundred customers, the founders realised there was a genuine demand for accessible mobility solutions in India. They expanded the design to fit nearly 80 percent of Indian car models before formally establishing TRUE Assistive Technology in 2022. Designing for Indian conditions As Anand began designing the products, one principle remained non-negotiable. "I didn't want to do anything like jugaad ," he says. Instead of permanently altering vehicles, the founders focused on creating solutions that could fit existing cars without affecting warranties, insurance, or resale value. Their flagship innovation, TurnPlus , is a patented swivel-seat mechanism that transforms an existing car seat into one that rotates outward. Rather than climbing or being lifted awkwardly into the vehicle, the passenger can first sit on the seat while it faces the door. The seat then swivels back into the cabin, making transfers smoother for senior citizens and people with conditions such as paralysis, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, post-polio complications and spinal injuries. Unlike many vehicle modifications that require structural changes, TurnPlus uses the car's existing seat. The mechanism is installed beneath it, allowing the seat to rotate without permanently altering the vehicle. TRUE Assistive Technology's portable ramps and transfer systems help wheelchair users navigate everyday barriers at home and on the move. "We didn't want people to leave their vehicles in garages for days," Naina explains. "You don't have to leave the vehicle with us. We bring the product to your doorstep." Because the original seat remains intact, the system can also be removed later if the owner decides to sell the vehicle, helping preserve its resale value. As they worked with more users, the founders realised that mobility challenges rarely end once someone gets into a car. Some wheelchair users needed a safer way to enter vehicles without being manually lifted. Others struggled with small staircases outside homes, clinics or public buildings. That led to the development of RamPlus , a lightweight portable ramp that can be carried in a vehicle and unfolded whenever a step or raised entrance blocks wheelchair access. The company later introduced TransPlus and HoistPlus , assistive systems and transferring devices that help caregivers lift and transfer people safely between wheelchairs, beds and vehicles, reducing physical strain for both users and families. For individuals who require more extensive support, TRUE also undertakes end-to-end vehicle modifications, including wheelchair ramps, hydraulic lifts and roof-height adjustments that convert standard vehicles into wheelchair-accessible ones. Before reaching users, every solution undergoes automotive safety testing, including front and rear crash tests, seat belt anchorage testing and durability assessments across temperatures ranging from minus 20 C to plus 60 C. The above tests are only for their products and not for vehicle modifications. "If I had to sell it across India , it had to be as reliable as the vehicle itself," Anand says. 'To be dependent on anybody is very painful' For Amritsar resident Jatin Gandotra, the technology came into his life after someone close to him suffered a stroke. His relative, now in her 60s, has severely restricted mobility and has spent nearly two years confined to bed. Jatin first discovered TRUE Assistive Technology while reading about a collaboration with Maruti Suzuki. "I found the technology very fascinating because my close relative is a stroke patient," he says. "I wanted to see how we could help her." After a relative suffered a stroke, Jatin Gandotra turned to accessible mobility to make family outings easier for her. Today, the family uses TurnPlus to help her get into the car more comfortably. Speaking about the emotional impact, Jatin says it goes far beyond the physical act of travelling. "To be dependent upon anybody is very, very painful," he says. "When you look through the patient's eyes, you can see that satisfaction that they are being cared for." For him, accessible mobility is ultimately about giving families more choices. "See what freedom you can bring to their life," he says. More than easier journeys The founders say stories like these continue to reinforce why they chose this path. Among their earliest customers was a woman who completed her PhD sooner because she could travel to college more frequently after installing the mobility solution. Another user, Vijay Kannan, fulfilled a long-held dream of driving his parents to Ayodhya after equipping his vehicle with an accessible ramp. "It's not just for the person using it," says Naina. "It helps the entire family. When they see how conveniently they can travel together, it changes things for everyone." Rashmi has witnessed that change firsthand. "The more we socialise these children, the happier they become," she says. "We shouldn't confine them to a single room." Her daughter now plans trips with the confidence many teenagers take for granted. "She says, 'We'll go anywhere. We'll explore this place.' She feels nothing is limited for her anymore." For families like Rashmi's, accessible mobility means fewer limitations, more shared experiences and the freedom to explore the world beyond their homes. According to the Census 2011, India is home to over 2.68 crore persons with disabilities, alongside a rapidly growing elderly population. Yet for many, something as ordinary as getting into a vehicle remains one of the biggest barriers to participating in everyday life. For families like Rashmi's and Jatin's, accessible mobility is not simply about modifying a car. It means visiting relatives without anxiety, travelling to school or work more comfortably, taking a long-awaited road trip, or stepping outside after months of staying indoors. Sometimes, restoring independence begins with making the first step into a vehicle a little easier. All images courtesy True Assistive Technology team

items.descriptionOriginal: Florida Polytechnic University is preparing to bring a piloted electric aircraft into law enforcement, opening a new front in aerial policing. Its police department plans to use a Jetson ONE aircraft, nicknamed Astro, for campus patrols and emergency response. The aircraft uses electric propulsion and vertical takeoff and landing capabilities. Those features could help officers reach locations that conventional patrol vehicles cannot easily access. However, the university still needs approval from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) before operational deployment. Electric flight enters policing Astro could give officers another way to monitor the university’s campus and surrounding grounds. Police Chief Aaron Murray also sees potential for emergency operations after severe weather. The aircraft could help teams assess affected areas and deliver essential supplies when roads become difficult to navigate. Florida Poly’s department also plans to work with other regional law enforcement agencies. Those partnerships could extend Astro’s role beyond campus security and support wider emergency response efforts. Murray believes police departments should understand emerging aviation technology before it becomes commonplace. He said the university wants to explore its potential for public safety and safer airspace operations. The aircraft’s arrival also reflects a broader shift in how law enforcement adopts new equipment. Drones have already become useful tools for police departments. Florida Poly now wants to investigate what a piloted electric aircraft can offer. Jetson skips waiting list California-based Jetson accelerated the university’s order despite a three-year waiting list for the Jetson ONE. CEO Stéphan D’haene said Florida Poly’s engineering focus and public safety objectives made the project a priority. Jetson has traditionally served recreational flight customers. D’haene said the company also wants to identify practical applications beyond leisure flying. The university’s plans offer an opportunity to test electric personal aircraft in a professional setting. The Jetson ONE features eight electric motors, a top speed of 63 mph, and an estimated flight time of 20 minutes. The single-seat aircraft weighs about 253 pounds with batteries and includes a ballistic parachute and an automatic landing function. Astro’s integration could provide a useful case study for the emerging advanced air mobility sector. That field explores new aircraft and operating models for moving people and equipment through the air. However, the university must first secure FAA authorization. That approval will determine when police can begin using the aircraft in official operations. Hands-on flight research Astro will also serve as an engineering research platform at Florida Poly. The university introduced an aerospace engineering degree this fall, giving students a direct connection to emerging aviation systems. Faculty and students plan to examine real-time operational data from the aircraft. They also expect to incorporate the information into senior capstone design projects. These efforts could expose students to practical engineering problems involving electric flight and aviation safety. Provost Brad Thiessen said the aircraft will give students and faculty a way to study real-world data. He added that the work could help them tackle engineering challenges associated with advanced air mobility. Florida Poly has already expanded its campus technology programs. Its police department recently added a drone unit, while students operate a cybersecurity-focused Security Operations Center. Astro extends that approach into piloted electric aviation . Its eventual deployment could help the university explore how emerging aircraft fit into policing, emergency management, and engineering education.

items.descriptionOriginal: Frankie Robertson had spent years helping families navigate premature birth. But nothing could have prepared her for sitting in a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) with her own newborn daughter. Robertson had spent nearly a decade in leadership at March of Dimes, an organization whose work includes premature birth prevention. She had listened to parents’ stories, supported families and cried alongside mothers whose babies arrived too soon. But experiencing it herself was entirely different, revealing a gap often overlooked in conversations about pregnancy and childbirth: Mothers need care and support long after their babies arrive. It’s a critical need that philanthropists Olivia and Tom Walton are working to address. In September 2026, the couple announced an initial $100 million commitment over five years to Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies America , a national initiative aiming to cut the country’s maternal mortality rate in half by 2031. The investment is intended to help states expand promising approaches to maternal healthcare, particularly in rural and underserved communities where women face significant barriers to care. That includes expanding access to virtual appointments for women who live far from healthcare providers, training more midwives and community health workers, and strengthening postpartum care during the critical first year after childbirth. Olivia Walton's 0 million dollar commitment to maternal health Rather than creating an entirely new healthcare system, the initiative aims to help states put proven solutions into practice on a larger scale. The Waltons’ $100 million commitment will support state matching grants, partnerships, and improvements in healthcare infrastructure , with the goal of attracting additional public and private investment to sustain those efforts long after the initial five years. The ultimate measure of success is ambitious but straightforward: cutting the nation’s maternal mortality rate in half by 2031. The risks aren’t the same for every mother The United States has one of the highest maternal mortality rates among wealthy nations, and those risks aren’t shared equally. In 2024, non-Hispanic Black women were more than three times as likely to die from maternal causes as non-Hispanic white women, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . This disparity is driven by a combination of systemic inequities in healthcare, including unequal access to quality prenatal and postpartum care, higher rates of certain underlying health conditions, and racial bias within the medical system. Research also shows that Black women’s concerns about their symptoms are sometimes dismissed or inadequately addressed by healthcare providers, potentially delaying lifesaving treatment. Geography matters, too. In rural communities, women may have to travel long distances to reach maternity care, making consistent prenatal and postpartum support difficult to access. Robertson, who has spent much of her career advocating for maternal health equity in Louisiana, believes improving outcomes also requires recognizing the circumstances women bring into pregnancy. Researchers call one aspect of this weathering : the cumulative physical toll of chronic stress, discrimination and systemic inequities. First proposed by public health researcher Arline Geronimus , the hypothesis explores how these experiences may contribute to poorer health outcomes over time. “It’s not simply about experiencing an isolated act of discrimination,” Robertson explained. “It’s about the overall effect, physiological toll of navigating just environments where you constantly have to confront, recover from inequities, or anticipate them.” Improving maternal health means looking beyond medical emergencies and recognizing the importance of consistent care, emotional support and access to resources before, during and after childbirth. What if better maternal care looked like this? Imagine a new mother returning home from the hospital, exhausted and overwhelmed. She’s anxious, struggling to sleep and unsure whether what she’s experiencing is a normal part of recovery or a sign that something is wrong. Now imagine someone comes to check on her. A postpartum home visit could help identify complications, answer questions and connect her with additional care. A midwife or community health worker could help another mother navigate appointments and find needed resources. A doula could provide emotional and practical support during childbirth, helping a woman understand her options and communicate her needs. Photo by Sarah Chai For mothers experiencing postpartum depression or anxiety, better access to mental health services could mean receiving help before symptoms become a crisis. These are among the approaches Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies America hopes to help states expand, building on programs already showing promise rather than starting from scratch. In October, the initiative announced its first state-level investments: $10 million each for Arkansas and Kentucky over five years. The grants are intended to strengthen maternal healthcare access, particularly in rural communities, through workforce development, postpartum support and improved maternal health data. The initiative hopes successful approaches can eventually be adopted in other states. Photo by Healthy Moms and Healthy Babies America The investments are still in their early stages, and it will take time to see how many families benefit and whether improvements can be sustained. The Waltons hope their commitment will also attract additional public and private funding to help effective services reach more communities beyond the initial five years. Helping mothers find joy, even when pregnancy doesn’t go as planned For Robertson, the importance of having someone looking out for mothers is deeply personal. Her experiences with postpartum recovery and her daughter’s premature birth inspired her to become a doula and establish Black Joy Doula Firm, a maternal health practice focused on supporting Black women through pregnancy and childbirth. Her goal is to help mothers facing unexpected complications manage their fears, understand their options and hold on to some of the joy they felt when they first imagined becoming parents. “I wanted to be a doula to work with moms who get this news and then show them how to protect their peace, help them with coping mechanisms, help them slow down, help them maintain that joy,” she explained. It’s a philosophy that reflects what meaningful maternal care should look like: someone who listens, recognizes when a mother needs help and understands that her well-being matters, too. Frankie Robertson at the Joyful Birth Advocacy session with expectant moms, partners, and families at the Community Baby Shower Robertson knows firsthand that even mothers with extensive knowledge and resources can find themselves overwhelmed by the unexpected. But protecting maternal health shouldn’t be a responsibility women carry alone. That’s what makes the Waltons’ investment an opportunity worth watching. If it helps more communities provide consistent, compassionate care, fewer mothers may have to navigate pregnancy and recovery without the support they deserve. Because when a baby arrives, a mother’s need for care doesn’t end. A healthier start for families begins with making sure someone is looking out for her, too. items.titleOriginal: Boeing’s largest 230-seat 737 MAX jet wins FAA approval after 2,000 flight hours
items.description: Η Ομοσπονδιακή Υπηρεσία Αεροπορίας (FAA) έχει πιστοποιήσει το 737 MAX 10 της Boeing, το μεγαλύτερο αεροσκάφος της οικογένειας 737 MAX, μετά από πρόγραμμα δοκιμών που περιλαμβάνει σχεδόν 1.000 πτήσεις και περισσότερες από 2.000 ώρες πτήσης. Η έγκριση ανοίγει το δρόμο για την Boeing να ξεκινήσει την παράδοση του 737-10 τους επόμενους μήνες. Το αεροσκάφος μπορεί να φιλοξενήσει έως και 230 περάσματα…
items.descriptionOriginal: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has certified Boeing’s 737 MAX 10, the largest aircraft in the 737 MAX family, following a testing program involving nearly 1,000 flights and more than 2,000 flight hours. The approval clears the path for Boeing to begin delivering the 737-10 in the coming months. The aircraft can accommodate up to 230 passengers, making it the highest-capacity model in the company’s single-aisle 737 MAX lineup. The certification follows extensive safety assessments, design reviews, and ground testing. Boeing said the program included 1,000 ground test hours, tens of thousands of pages of documentation and formal reviews with the FAA. The 737-10 is also the first commercial aircraft certified under the full requirements of the 2020 Aircraft Certification, Safety, and Accountability Act. The law introduced stricter requirements for documenting aircraft safety assessments and evaluating how pilots interact with aircraft systems. New safety requirements apply What sets the aircraft apart is its enhanced angle-of-attack system, which Boeing plans to introduce across the 737 MAX family. Angle of attack refers to the angle between an aircraft wing and the airflow approaching it. The measurement helps pilots and onboard systems assess flight conditions, including the risk of an aerodynamic stall. Boeing says the upgraded system is designed to reduce pilot workload. Its introduction across the MAX family makes the 737-10 an important step in the company’s broader aircraft safety program. “Our flight test team ran a disciplined, methodical campaign to validate every system,” said Chris Payne, vice president and general manager of 737 Airplane Development Programs at Boeing Commercial Airplanes. Larger aircraft expands capacity The 737-10 typically seats between 185 and 210 passengers in a two-class configuration, although its maximum seating capacity reaches 230. The aircraft has a range of up to 3,100 nautical miles (5,740 kilometers). Boeing also claims it offers the lowest cost per seat among single-aisle aircraft currently in service, although that comparison was not independently established in the announcement. According to Boeing , the aircraft offers 365 nautical miles more range than competing aircraft without auxiliary fuel tanks. The company also says technological improvements across the 737 MAX program reduce fuel consumption and carbon dioxide emissions by 20%, without specifying the comparison baseline in the announcement. Airline interest in the largest MAX variant is substantial. Boeing reported 1,555 orders from more than 30 customers, representing over 30 percent of the program’s outstanding orders. Across the broader 737 MAX family, customers have placed 7,350 orders, with nearly 2,500 aircraft delivered through September 2026. The FAA certified the smaller 737-7 earlier this year. With the 737-10 now approved, Boeing has secured certification for the final member of the MAX family . However, certification does not mean the aircraft has entered commercial service. Boeing expects customer deliveries to begin in the coming months.

items.title: Οι μπαταρίες EV θα μπορούσαν να μειώσουν το αποτύπωμα άνθρακα κατά 34% έως το 2050, αποκαλύπτει νέα μελέτη
items.titleOriginal: EV batteries could cut their carbon footprint 34% by 2050, new study reveals
items.description: Οι εκπομπές της εφοδιαστικής αλυσίδας μπαταριών ιόντων λιθίου θα μπορούσαν να μειωθούν κατά περίπου 34 τοις εκατό έως το 2050, σύμφωνα με μια νέα μελέτη από ερευνητές στο Πανεπιστήμιο της Μελβούρνης. Σύμφωνα με τη μελέτη, αυτό θα μπορούσε να επιτευχθεί συνδυάζοντας την καθαρότερη κατασκευή με στρατηγικές που μειώνουν τον αριθμό των μπαταριών που χρειάζεται ο κόσμος. Οι ερευνητές διαπίστωσαν ότι κατά την απανθρακοποίηση…
items.descriptionOriginal: Lithium-ion battery supply-chain emissions could be cut by roughly 34 percent by 2050, a new study by researchers at the University of Melbourne found. According to the study, this could be achieved by combining cleaner manufacturing with strategies that reduce the number of batteries the world needs. The researchers found that while decarbonizing battery production is still essential, demand-side measures, including prolonging battery life, limiting the growth of EV battery sizes, promoting ride-sharing, and repurposing used batteries for energy storage, could deliver even greater emissions reductions than manufacturing improvements alone. Reseachers noted that demand for lithium-ion batteries is expected to soar over the coming decades as electric vehicles (EVs) replace gasoline-powered cars and green energy systems require large-scale electricity storage. While agreeing that batteries play a key role in cutting emissions from transport and power generation, the study warns that emissions from producing them could rise sharply if manufacturing expands without cleaner processes. Cleaner battery production To assess future impacts, the researchers modeled greenhouse gas emissions across the battery life cycle, from raw resource extraction and manufacturing to recycling, for batteries used in EVs and stationary energy storage through 2050. The analysis included regional differences in electricity generation and battery demand using International Energy Agency scenarios. The study found that on the supply side, the carbon footprint of an individual battery could be reduced by about 34 percent by 2050. The change can be brought about by shifting to cleaner manufacturing, improved production efficiency, lower-carbon battery chemistries, and expanded recycling. The researchers, however, found an even greater potential to reduce battery demand without slowing electrification. In their analysis, researchers found that by ensuring EV batteries last as long as the vehicles they power, the battery demand could be slashed by 29 percent, while limiting the continued growth in average battery pack capacity could cut demand by another 23 percent. Wider adoption of carpooling services could reduce demand by nearly 10 percent, and repurposing retired EV batteries for stationary energy storage could lower demand by a further 8 percent. Together, these measures could eliminate 6–7.2 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions between 2024 and 2050. Recycling cuts emissions Recycling also plays an important role in lowering the ecological burden of batteries. A separate Stanford University analysis published in 2025 found that recovering battery materials from manufacturing scrap and spent batteries produces less than half the greenhouse gas emissions of conventional mining and refining. Recycling also uses about one-quarter of the water and energy required to extract new metals, with the greatest benefits achieved when processing manufacturing scrap. The researchers said the findings highlighted that the battery industry should focus on making cleaner batteries while pushing better use of every battery produced. As global demand continues to rise, strategies that extend battery life, encourage reuse, and expand recycling could significantly reduce the climate cost of the clean energy transition.

items.title: Ζευγάρι στην Καλιφόρνια ταξίδεψε σε 33 χώρες φωτογραφίζοντας κάθε είδος άγριων γατών στη Γη
items.titleOriginal: California Couple Has Traveled to 33 Countries Photographing Every Wild Cat Species on Earth
items.description: Ένα παντρεμένο ζευγάρι από την Καλιφόρνια έχει κάνει αποστολή του να φωτογραφίσει και τα 40 είδη άγριων γατών στη Γη — και έχουν μόνο ένα ακόμα μπροστά τους. Οι εκπληκτικές εικόνες χρησιμεύουν για την ευαισθητοποίηση σχετικά με τα ζώα, πολλά από τα οποία είναι ευάλωτα ή απειλούνται με εξαφάνιση. Μέχρι στιγμής, ο Sebastian Kennerknecht και η Rachel Tobias έχουν ταξιδέψει σε 33 χώρες σε πέντε ηπείρους και…
items.descriptionOriginal: A married California couple has made it their mission to photograph all 40 wild cat species on Earth — and they only have one more to go. The stunning images serve to raise awareness about the animals, many of which are vulnerable or endangered. So far, Sebastian Kennerknecht and Rachel Tobias have traveled to 33 countries across five continents and photographed 39 species in the Felidae family, often using camera traps in forests, deserts, and grasslands where the elusive cats roam. SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht The San Francisco-based duo has captured images of a cheetah in Tanzania, a tiger in India, and an ocelot in Panama. The only species they have yet to cross off the list is the northern oncilla, found in Central America. It’s a rarely seen animal, and one of smallest wild cats in the Americas. View this post on Instagram Kennerknecht, 41, has been photographing cats since college: He studied ecology at the University of California, Santa Cruz, to understand animals and became particularly interested in bobcats. Tobias, 37, grew up loving wildlife and was always drawn to the ocean and photography. The two met online, and they instantly connected over their love of nature. Fittingly, their first date was searching for bobcats. SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht In 2024, Kennerknecht realized he had photos of 30 of the world’s wild cats, so he and Tobias decided to go for the full 40. In addition to photography, the couple run cat expeditions together, taking out small groups to observe the felines in their natural habitat and learn how to photograph them. They’ve raised hundreds of thousands of dollars through their work. One photo of a Borneo Bay cat brought in $120,000 for conservation efforts, and they collected around $70,000 per year for five years to protect lion species in Zambia’s Kafue National Park. They are partnered with Panthera, the world’s leading wild cat conservation organization. Kennerknecht told Talk to the Press that the couple’s work is “99% frustration and 1% joy,” noting that they’ve seen elephants crush their expensive camera traps, insects get into them, and humidity fog up lenses, rendering images unusable. “We set up a studio in the forest,” Tobias explained, adding: “In Malaysia, we set up six traps; we had to sleep in the jungle full of bugs and carry 60 pounds of gear.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht Despite the project’s challenges, the couple is dedicated to ethical photography. They don’t use any bait or lures to attract the cats towards the cameras, so they can observe their natural behavior. “It’s much more successful for telling a story about the species,” said Tobias. “Telling a story between the viewer and the animal is really powerful for conservation.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht A large part of their aim is to introduce the world to the 33 small wild cat species that are relatively unknown, so more can be done to protect them. “If you protect small cats, you protect big cats,” she added. The pair also wants to prove humans can coexist with big and small wild cats. “There are lots of human activities that might negatively impact cats without people knowing,” Tobias said. “People want to protect natural spaces and help with coexistence.” View this post on Instagram In Paraguay at the time of this writing, the team has had camera traps set up since April to capture the northern oncilla, with a ground crew frequently checking on them, but the cat has remained elusive. View this post on Instagram “It’s been pretty incredible,” Kennerknecht said, “but measuring local awareness has been tough.” They’ve set up billboards in areas with wild cats, featuring pictures of the local cats with the slogan, “I’m your neighbor.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht As for their favorite species, Kennerknecht said his is a bobcat, as that’s the feline that launched his photographic journey in Santa Cruz. But for Tobias: “There’s nothing more beautiful than a female leopard.” SWNS / Sebastian Kennerknecht Below are the cats they’ve photographed so far: Lion — Zambia Jaguar — Brazil Tiger — India Snow Leopard — Kyrgyzstan Leopard — Zambia Mainland Clouded Leopard — Malaysia Sunda Clouded Leopard — Malaysia African Golden Cat — Uganda Caracal — Yemen Serval — Tanzania Geoffroy’s Cat — Argentina Southern Oncila — Brazil Andean Mountain Cat- Argentina Pampas Cat- Bolivia Ocelot — Panama Margay — Panama Marbled Cat — Malaysia Borneo Bay Cat — Malaysia Asiatic Golden Cat — Indonesia Bobcat — U.S. Canada Lynx — Canada Eurasian Lynx — Kyrgyzstan Iberian Lynx — Spain Mountain Lion — Chile Cheetah — Tanzania Mainland Leopard Cat — Malaysia Sunda Leopard Cat — Malaysia Flat-Headed Cat — Malaysia Rusty-Spotted Cat — India Fishing Cat — Thailand Pallas’s Cat — Mongolia Jungle Cat — India Sand Cat — Western Sahara Black-footed Cat — South Africa European Wild Cat — Spain Afro-Asiatic Wild Cat — Botswana Chinese Mountain Cat — China Jaguarundi — Location Unconfirmed/South America Güiña — Location Unconfirmed/Chile/Argentina This article was originally written by William Ormes Roder for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.title: Ένας επιστήμονας του Χάρβαρντ παρακολουθούσε «ντροπαλά» μωρά για 13 χρόνια. Αυτό που βρήκε είναι ένα χρυσωρυχείο για τους γονείς.
items.titleOriginal: A Harvard scientist followed ‘shy’ babies for 13 years. What he found is a goldmine for parents.
items.description: Ο ψυχολόγος του Χάρβαρντ Τζερόμ Κάγκαν είχε μια άκαμπτη άποψη για τη φύση εναντίον της ανατροφής νωρίς στην καριέρα του: «Μπήκα στην ψυχολογία γιατί ήθελα να ανακαλύψω πόσο ισχυρό ήταν το περιβάλλον και ήμουν πολύ απρόθυμος να αναγνωρίσω τον ρόλο οποιωνδήποτε βιολογικών διαφορών μεταξύ των παιδιών», λέει σε μια συνέντευξη στο κανάλι YouTube The Brainwaves Video Anthology.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Harvard psychologist Jerome Kagan had a rigid view on nature vs nurture early in his career: “I entered psychology because I wanted to discover how powerful the environment was and I was very reluctant to acknowledge the role of any biological differences between children,” he says in an interview with The Brainwaves Video Anthology YouTube channel. But the more he studied upbringing, family life, and other environmental factors, the more he felt he was missing a piece of the bigger picture of what shapes a child’s temperament, whether they are shy or outgoing. Harvard psychologists followed infants and toddlers for years to uncover the roots of shyness Kagan says he could see differences between infants of different nationalities at just 3 months old, which led him to realize that our natural temperament must have a biological underpinning. So in the late 1970s, he launched a series of studies following what he called both “high reactive” and “low reactive” children. Researchers screened infants as young as four months for how much they reacted to unfamiliar stimuli. This could be as simple as introducing a new toy or mobile, or taking them to an unfamiliar place. “High reactive” kids would cry and flail, while “low reactive” kids would be mostly unbothered. The most extreme cases on both ends of the spectrum were selected for long-term follow-ups over the course of several years, with many children being studied well into their adolescence, and some into adulthood. All-in-all, Kagan studied temperament for decades, and much of what he discovered helped write the so-called book on shy kids. Here are a few of the most interesting bits of his research: Being “shy” is mostly physiological Kagan found that infants only three or four months old could be easily sorted into the high or low reactive bucket. His research eventually revealed that shyness, or high reactivity, stems from an overactive or hypersensitive nervous system. Physical differences in brain makeup and neurochemistry make some people more attuned to stimulation. Kagan could quite literally see the difference through activity in the amygdala, the part of the brain responsible for our survival instincts and fight-or-flight response. Previous research had pegged shyness as a fixed personality trait, but Kagan’s long-term studies revealed that it is often biologically based and inherited, which is a total game-changer. In some cases, he found that people could “develop” shyness over time due to trauma at home or other environmental factors. But shyness, or being “inhibited,” is not locked in place One of the most fascinating parts of Kagan’s long-term research was how it clearly showed that shyness can change over time. Even though its basis lies in our nervous system and brain chemistry, the children he studied sometimes became less shy and reactive over time—and sometimes more. “I would say, if you start with 10 very shy children at age 1, you’ll end up with 3 who are very shy as adolescents,” he said in 1991, per The Harvard Crimson . The most extreme cases were the least likely to change. Shy kids can learn to be bold adults, but the brain markers remain One major follow-up in Kagan’s work was doing brain scans, some 20 years later, on some of the children he identified early on as shy or highly reactive. He found that many of those kids had become less “fearful” as adults. They had learned to overcome their shyness and be bolder. However, their brains still showed a highly active, sensitive amygdala upon scanning. This not only supported his original theories that shyness is biological, but it also showed that many of these kids eventually learned coping strategies and social skills that helped them overcome their natural temperament. The key to parenting a shy child Understanding shyness as an inherited but flexible physiological trait, and not a rigid one, goes a long way toward understanding kids who are more sensitive than their peers. It helps us see that reserved kids aren’t being difficult or stubborn—they just have a stronger physical reaction to things that wouldn’t faze an “uninhibited child.” However, parents, teachers, and anyone else who regularly interacts with kids want to know the best way to engage a shy child. Kagan says pushing them too hard and forcing them out of their comfort zone is the worst thing you can do. “You have to be sensitive. You don’t want to put too much pressure on such children to join the group and be sociable,” he said in the Crimson . However, gentle encouragement and help building scaffolding for social skills, coping strategies, and confidence can go a long way. Kagan specifically advocated making the unfamiliar familiar: meeting the teacher in advance, touring a new classroom before the first day, and exposing students to new things whenever possible. Shy brains may always tell a person that the world is threatening, but they can learn to adjust the way they act on that feeling. There’s a correlation between shyness and blue eyes The shy kids Kagan studied were also more likely to have blue eyes, he noted. He even theorized that the genetic factors that determine our eye color may be the same ones that influence how sensitive our nervous system is to stimulation. However, follow-up studies have either failed to find the same correlation or found it fairly weak. Kagan also found that the inhibited kids he studied were likely to grow up tall and thin and suffer from conditions like hay fever and eczema due to higher levels of stress hormones. The magic number for parents Shyness isn’t inherently bad; Kagan was careful never to treat it as a disorder or something that needed fixing. In fact, a shy temperament often helps people succeed in fields that value being measured, careful, and a good listener. In extreme cases, however, a sensitive temperament can lead to adults who are fearful, isolated, or who suffer from anxiety disorders. Moreover, modern society tends to reward people who are outgoing, bold, and extroverted. Kagan says the key to helping a child overcome a shy temperament is early intervention, ideally before age 7. “The general rule [is], you change a lot between birth and age 7. After age 7, you don’t change very much. If you’re extremely shy and fearful at 7–the odds are about two-thirds of those kids will be shy as adolescents,” he says. A stigma still remains around people who are labeled as shy. People often conflate shyness or reserve with fear, weakness, or a lack of confidence. Kagan’s work went a long way toward clearing up misunderstandings about what shyness is and isn’t, but we could all use a bit of a refresher. A shy temperament is the result of a brain that’s hypersensitive to danger, not a failure of parents to socialize or a child being stubborn or difficult. But temperament and behavior are two different things, and with the right support, many extremely shy kids can go on to become highly social and successful adults. The post A Harvard scientist followed ‘shy’ babies for 13 years. What he found is a goldmine for parents. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Τα σκυλιά συνεχίζουν να χτυπούν τα πόδια στην τηλεόραση κατά τη διάρκεια ενός συγκεκριμένου καρτούν του Netflix… που δεν ήταν φτιαγμένο για αυτούς. Ένα νοτιοκορεατικό καρτούν για μια αποικία φώκιες έχει μετατραπεί σε απροσδόκητη επιτυχία με ζώα και τα μέσα κοινωνικής δικτύωσης είναι γεμάτα βίντεο με σκυλιά να στέκονται ίντσες από την οθόνη, να γέρνουν το κεφάλι τους και να χτυπούν το γυαλί. Μια γυναίκα από το Όρεγκον είπε στον Guardian ότι α…
items.descriptionOriginal: Dogs keep pawing at the TV during a specific Netflix cartoon … that wasn’t made for them. A South Korean cartoon about a colony of seals has turned into an unexpected hit with animals, and social media is full of videos of dogs standing inches from the screen, tilting their heads and batting at the glass . One Oregon woman told The Guardian that a clip of her two goldendoodles watching it pulled nearly 10 million views. “The minute the seals started drumming, Benny sat up, and Myrtle had these subtle head tilts,” she said. The show is Sealook , a wordless slapstick series co-produced by The Pinkfong Company and Million Volt. It premiered in South Korea in 2022 and later landed on Netflix, where it’s listed as a TV-Y kids’ comedy. It was made for children. “Seeing cats and now dogs as well, becoming so absorbed in Sealook has been a fun and unexpected surprise,” Leah Yeon, Pinkfong’s communications lead, told The Guardian . She said they didn’t set out to make a show for animals, but what they did make is pretty (and accidentally), perfect for one. Dogs and cats are dichromatic , meaning they see blues and yellows well but struggle to distinguish reds and greens. Sealook is pale ice, blue water, and brightly colored seals, so almost the entire color palette falls inside the range an animal can actually distinguish. Netflix noted in its own feature on the show that viewers started pointing this out in late summer, and that it’s a coincidence rather than a design choice. Then there’s the movement on the screen. “Cats and dogs are particularly interested in movement because they are instinctively drawn to chasing a mouse or other prey,” David Williams, an associate lecturer in veterinary ophthalmology at the University of Cambridge, told The Guardian . Freya Mowat, a veterinary ophthalmologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, put it more plainly to the paper: “Cartoons are great content for dogs: high contrast, lots of movement, nice fun music, it’s the whole package.” The sound may matter as much as the picture. Emily Blackwell, a companion-animal behavior specialist, told The Guardian that the noises the seals make could register as prey sounds or as squeaky toys. Williams suggested an easy at-home test: turn the sound off and see whether your dog stays interested. A 2024 study in Applied Animal Behaviour Science surveyed 1,246 dog owners and found that 86% said their dogs watched screens, with 90% of those owners citing movement as what grabbed the dog’s attention and 78% citing sound. However, that study is about dogs and screens in general, not this show—and it says nothing about cats. Nobody has actually tested Sealook on a representative sample of animals. But what does exist is a pile of videos of pets that do appear to be watching, and a reasonable enough theory about why. Of course, plenty of dogs don’t care at all. As one commenter put it: “I put this on for my dog, and she’s watching me instead.” The post Pets are pawing at screens to watch this South Korean cartoon. Experts explain the science behind it. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Η Hilary Swank ανταποκρίνεται τέλεια στη γυναίκα που λέει ότι είναι πολύ μεγάλη για να κάνει παιδιά
items.titleOriginal: Hilary Swank responds perfectly to woman who says she’s too old to have kids
items.description: Η ηθοποιός Hilary Swank περιμένει το τρίτο της παιδί. Η 52χρονη σταρ του Boys Don’t Cry ανακοίνωσε την εγκυμοσύνη της στο Instagram στις 14 Οκτωβρίου μαζί με τον σύζυγό της, Philip Schneider, και τα δίδυμα (γιος Ohm και κόρη Aya). Η Swank έγινε για πρώτη φορά μαμά στα 48. Κατά τη διάρκεια μιας πρόσφατης εμφάνισης στο The Drew Barrymore Show, η Swank μίλησε για το πώς είναι να είσαι έγκυος…
items.descriptionOriginal: Actress Hilary Swank is expecting her third child. The Boys Don’t Cry star, 52, announced her pregnancy on Instagram on October 14 alongside her husband, Philip Schneider, and twins (son Ohm and daughter Aya). Swank became a first-time mom at 48. During a recent appearance on The Drew Barrymore Show , Swank opened up about what it’s like to be pregnant at 52. “I just entered my third trimester,” she told Barrymore. Swank’s pregnancy at 52 As the two sat down together, Swank shared that the last time she appeared on Barrymore’s show, she was 12 weeks pregnant with her twins. “Now with this baby I’m 28 weeks,” Swank said before adding, “Just one this time!” They continue to talk about Swank’s pregnancy cravings (which include Rice Krispies Treats and a vegan alternative to Cheetos) before Barrymore reiterates how “beautiful, glowing, gorgeous” Swank looks. “It’s amazing what women’s bodies can do, and it’s just such an extraordinary privilege and honor and blessing to carry life. It’s a dream come true and I love being a mom,” said Swank. Barrymore asks Swank to share more about what it was like to share her first pregnancy with the world at an “older age.” “This was the right time for me. Although not everything happens in our own time. We have ideas for timelines for ourselves, and getting pregnant isn’t always in our own timeline, right?” Swank shared. “You can hope and pray for certain things, and things happen when they’re supposed to happen. I was very excited, and it was a good time for me because I feel like I had this career that was a ‘baby’ of mine that I really wanted to give to and devote my time to and not share. And now I can totally devote [myself] to my children.” View this post on Instagram “Backlash” for older pregnancies Swank continued, “What’s interesting and beautiful is a lot of people say, ‘This has given me hope that I can get pregnant too, and it’s something that I really want in my life,’ because for a lot of women it’s a ticking clock. It’s not the same for men.” Swank then talked about the “backlash women get for having children older but not men, which is interesting.” Barrymore chimed in that men “have babies in their 80s,” and when Swank had babies in her 40s, “people weren’t always gracious about it.” Swank responded with a story about criticism she received from a woman who told her, “How dare you! You’re too old. You won’t be [young] enough when your kids are older. My dad was my favorite person, and he died when I was in my early 20s. And it’s just devastation.” She added that she “related” to the woman’s story and was “drawn to it” after her father died at a young age as well. But then she thought to herself, “I would rather be born and have that person and experience that than not at all.” View this post on Instagram Becoming a mom at 48 In a 2024 interview with PEOPLE , Swank opened up about why getting pregnant at 47 and welcoming her twins at 48 was right for her. “I was 47 when I got pregnant, and I feel like I have a lot more patience, and I’ve done a lot of my own personal work to be the type of mother I want to be, whereas it would’ve just been different in my twenties and thirties,” she told the publication. “I don’t think I would’ve had the patience and the grace that I hopefully can bestow a little bit more [of] now, and a self-awareness in a different way that I don’t need to focus on myself anymore in the way that I did at that point,” she said. “I can give differently.” The post Hilary Swank responds perfectly to woman who says she’s too old to have kids appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Όποιος έχει παίξει Monopoly ξέρει πώς πάει συνήθως: αυτό που ξεκινά ως διασκεδαστικό παιχνίδι μετατρέπεται αναπόφευκτα σε ένα ατελείωτο slog μέχρι να συμφωνήσουν όλοι να ανακηρύξουν κάποιον νικητή. Ένας YouTuber που περνάει από το @sblga εξηγεί ότι, παρά το fo…
items.descriptionOriginal: Anyone who’s played Monopoly knows how it usually goes: what starts as a fun game inevitably turns into an endless slog until everyone agrees to declare someone the winner . As it turns out, we’ve brought this agony on ourselves by not actually following the official Monopoly game rules . A YouTuber who goes by @sblga explains says that, despite following all kinds of made-up “house rules,” most of us neglect one simple, official Monopoly rule that makes the game go much faster. It’s known as the “auction rule,” and it’s literally a game-changer. (By the way, he also shares the game’s absolutely wild history, which is definitely worth sticking around for.) How the ‘auction rule’ in Monopoly changes the game Several scenarios can trigger the auction rule. The primary rule, however, is that when a player lands on a property and doesn’t want to (or can’t) buy it, the property immediately goes up for auction, and all players can bid on it. There is no minimum bid, so bidding can start at just $1. Theoretically, if a player lands on Boardwalk and doesn’t buy it, another player (or even that original player) could nab it for far less than its $400 value through a bidding war. Players flush with cash can create monopolies simply by outbidding their opponents. This rule means properties get picked up much more quickly, so the game doesn’t stall. It also forces players to strategize differently with their property purchases and money management. Can you imagine playing a full game of Monopoly in 30 minutes and having someone actually win? It’s possible with the auction rule. Who knew? Monopoly money changing hands. Photo credit: Canva Monopoly ‘house rules’ ease the game’s ruthlessness So if the auction rule has always been part of the standard game rules, why don’t more people use it? Theories abound, but one big one is that most people just don’t read the official rules. Gameplay often gets passed down by family and friends, and for Monopoly in particular, “house rules” often trump official rules. Some popular Monopoly house rules include: Free Parking jackpot, in which all tax payments go to the center of the board instead of to the bank. When someone lands on Free Parking, they collect the jackpot. Double salary landing on GO. First-lap immunity, meaning no one can buy property on their first lap around the board. No rent in jail, meaning if a player is in jail, they cannot collect rent when other players land on their properties. People may not even realize that house rules aren’t standard. Someone likely eliminated the auction rule at some point to slow the game’s pace and/or reduce its brutality, and it spread and stuck. What’s interesting about Monopoly house rules is that they often ease the game’s ruthlessness, which is ironic, considering why the game was created in the first place. Monopoly’s origin story: A caution against unbridled capitalism In January of 1904, a woman named Lizzie Magie patented a game called the Landlord’s Game. The game had two sets of rules: one used a single land tax and distributed wealth among players, resulting in a collective win, and the other let players build monopolies and ruthlessly fleece opponents. It was meant to be a lesson, an indictment of unbridled capitalism. However, a heater salesman named Charles Darrow took a particular liking to the game and its monopoly rules. Without crediting the Landlord’s Game, Darrow created Monopoly as we know it and sold it to Parker Brothers. “What Magie intended as a forecast of disaster became Monopoly’s sole objective,” Public Domain Review notes. A criticism of greed and power imbalance became a celebration of free-market capitalism. In 1935, Parker Brothers bought Magie’s patent for $500 and no royalties . Meanwhile, Darrow became a millionaire. The tendency to add house rules to make Monopoly more fun and fair for everyone is a good sign. It may not be the original creators’ intention. Still, many prefer a “compassionate capitalism” version of the game (even if it does take five hours and no one really ever wins). The post Man explains the official Monopoly rule no one uses that ends the game way faster appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Life is a little easier now for a southern ground hornbill in the Netherlands, thanks to 3D-printed prostheses for his upper and lower beak. The turkey-sized bird at the ARTIS Amsterdam Royal Zoo suffered a severe injury that broke both sections of his bill and left him with two stumps, making it difficult for him to pick up food and groom himself. “He managed reasonably well with them, but he could no longer do everything a hornbill naturally does,” ARTIS veterinarian Martine van Zijll Langhout said in a press release . To improve his well-being, the team perfected custom prostheses that are “virtually identical” to his original beak. “A bird uses its beak all day long, to pick up food and, for example, to preen its plumage. Especially with a young bird that can still live to a very old age, we felt it was important to see if we could improve its quality of life,” van Zijll Langhout added. ARTIS Although several birds have been fitted with artificial beaks, this hornbill is believed to be the first to receive replacements for both the upper and lower beak. Should the beak parts continue to function well for the long-term, the team plans to publish a scientific paper detailing exactly how they created the prostheses, so veterinarians around the world can help similar patients. The process is technically complex, as every bird has a unique beak that perfectly aligns to its skull and other anatomy. If the shape isn’t exactly right for either part of the bill, the animal will struggle to use the prosthesis. To ensure their creation would be a success, van Zijll Langhout and her colleagues performed a CT scan of the bird’s head as well as the broken beak pieces. The prostheses were then 3D-printed from plastic, and orthopedic surgeons meticulously attached them using titanium components. View this post on Instagram One of the biggest risks with a procedure like this is that the bird will reject the new beak, which could result in the animal refusing to eat. The zoo staff planned for that possibility and were prepared to have the prostheses removed if need be — but so far, all is going well: The team reported the bird settled in right away after the beak attachment operation and even appeared to be “smiling” afterward . And the day following the surgery, he began eating independently. “That was an incredibly important moment for us,” said van Zijll Langhout. “He understood that he could use his beak and began to discover for himself what was possible with it.” RELATED: From a Dolphin’s Tail to a Bird’s Beak: 7 Innovative Prosthetics That Have Helped Animals

items.descriptionOriginal: The treatment delivers a light-sensitive algae protein to the retina. Paired with special goggles, it can restore limited vision and lasts for years. The patients sit perfectly still as a needle inches toward one of their eyes. After the injection, they’ll no longer be completely human. The syringe is filled with a gene therapy that installs a light-sensitive algae protein into failing retinas and could reboot some lost vision. When scientists first proposed using algae proteins to restore human eyesight, the idea seemed like science fiction. Could alien proteins integrate into our intricate visual system? Even if they did, could the brain translate the resulting signals into sight, rather than nonsensical bursts of light? A new study suggests yes, with caveats. The team treated people with retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic disease that gradually destroys light-sensing cells in the retina. Seven of ten patients showed improved light sensitivity. After patients donned goggles that deliver pulses of light to activate the algae proteins, the team tested their eyesight. Roughly half could reach for and touch objects or identify the orientation of a black bar, a common test of visual recovery. The treatment is still far from restoring full vision. What patients saw was too blurry and the field of view too narrow to discern texture or fine detail. The boundaries of objects looked squiggly. But those who responded to the treatment continued to improve over roughly five years. One participant, whose story made headlines in 2021 , can now recognize and count different objects, and white stripes on a crosswalk pop out. The study, called PIONEER , is an ambitious clinical trial combining gene therapy with optogenetics. The first goal was to assess safety, and it met the mark. Most participants experienced a brief bout of inflammation in the eye receiving the injection. The only patient to suffer a severe side effect was quickly treated with medication. The findings suggest the initial success wasn’t a fluke. The study “represents an important milestone for optogenetic vision restoration,” said study author Stefan Futterknecht at the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel, in a press release . Setting Sights High Around two decades ago, Karl Deisseroth was hunting for new ways to control brain cells. Electrical bursts and chemicals, which are how neurons communicate, seemed like obvious choices. But nature had something stranger to offer: algae. Algae produce a protein called channelrhodopsin. When activated by light, the protein changes neuron activity using a mechanism that works similarly in mammalian cells. In a foundational paper , Deisseroth’s team inserted the protein into rodent neurons, and voilá—the neurons could now be controlled using light. The technology, called optogenetics, revolutionized neuroscience. By genetically tagging specific neurons with channelrhodopsin, scientists can now dial the cells’ activity up or down like a dimmer switch. Optogenetic experiments have revealed brain circuits that shape feelings, memory, and cognition with unprecedented precision. Researchers panning for more genes in different algae strains struck gold again. One channelrhodopsin variant they found, ChrimsonR, was particularly exciting. Unlike the classic version that’s activated by blue light, ChrimsonR responds to amber light, which penetrates tissues better and is less damaging. More recently, scientists have begun to use generative AI to redesign natural proteins to make them even more sensitive to light. “Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, when the technology won the coveted prize this year. Still, it has mainly been considered a research tool. Light It Up Retinitis pigmentosa gradually robs people of their eyesight. Researchers have linked over 100 genetic variations to the condition, which kills off light-sensitive cells in the retina. “The replacement (or editing) of a single gene would not help most persons,” wrote Deisseroth in the New England Journal of Medicine . Instead, adding channelrhodopsin could offer a more universal solution by rewiring surviving neurons. Early successes bolstered the idea. In one study , scientists equipped cones—a type of retinal light-sensing cell—with channelrhodopsin in mice with retinitis pigmentosa. The therapy boosted their light sensitivity. It also reactivated cones that had stopped responding to light in human retina samples. The new study took a different approach. In advanced disease, cones may have already degenerated beyond the point at which they could be saved. So instead, the gene therapy targeted ganglion cells. These cells process signals from light-sensitive cells and pass that information to the brain, but don’t detect light themselves. Ganglion cells are, however, more resilient than cones. Add channelrhodopsin, and they could become substitute light sensors. The team packed genetic instructions for ChrimsonR into a harmless viral delivery system and injected it into the poorer seeing eye of 10 patients aged 40 to 73. All were legally blind, and each received one of three escalating doses. As the patients gradually built up levels of the algae protein in their eyes, the team faced another challenge: Translating visual scenes from the outside world into amber light that the engineered ganglion cells could recognize. They developed specialized goggles that look a bit like Apple’s Vision Pro. The goggles use a camera to scan the field of view thousands of times per second, monitoring for light changes in every pixel. When the device detects a change, it pulses amber light from that pixel into the eye. Because our eyes naturally dart around—often without us noticing—this dynamic method may better mimic normal vision. With the goggles on, 6 of 10 participants showed clinically meaningful improvement in light sensitivity, with more than a fourfold boost over baseline readings. One participant improved over 62-fold. Of the eight who agreed to further eyesight tests, roughly half could touch a notebook, grab a small staple box, and detect changes in a rotating bar. Of those who initially responded to the treatment, improvements lasted for years. Their brains also seemed to adapt to the alien light sensors. In one test, participants were asked to open or close their eyes while looking at a tumbler. Electrical brain signals related to vision were more coherent with eyes open, suggesting their perception depended on improved visual input. Any gene therapy carries risk. In an already worsening eye, inflammation and other side effects could cause further damage. Overall, the injection appeared relatively safe. Most participants experienced a temporary increase in eye pressure, but no detectable side effects throughout the body. The retina’s overall structure remained unchanged. One person suffered a blockage in a major eye artery that cleared within minutes after treatment with an FDA-approved eye drop. For now, the participants still can’t read or see faces. The therapy reaches only a fraction of their ganglion cells, making sharper vision harder to restore. More advanced versions of channelrhodopsin with greater light sensitivity may increase resolution. As for the hardware, the team is working on versions of the goggles that deliver more accurate and timely stimulation. Potential upgrades include an eye tracker, software to preprocess visual scenes, and even holographs . “Overall, although optogenetic methods have been developed primarily for basic science discovery,” wrote Deisseroth, they’re now heading towards “diverse therapeutic approaches.” The post Blind Patients Recover Partial Vision in Gene Therapy Trial appeared first on SingularityHub .

items.descriptionOriginal: If you’ve ever seen pictures of a stranger’s wedding and thought, “That looks like a good time! Wish I could’ve been there,” this article is for you. And if you’re in the market to get married and worried about paying for it , you might want to pay attention as well. Here’s the scenario: in the weeks or days leading up to their wedding , a couple finds that a handful of their guests have canceled. They’ve already purchased the meal, and arrangements have already been made for their attendance. The couple will have to eat the cost, and with weddings already averaging over $30,000 , who can afford the waste? What if there were a simple solution to that problem? View this post on Instagram Having strangers pay to attend your wedding Not a Wedding Crasher might be one of the most unique wedding businesses ever. The website describes the premise as “A thoughtful way to share the seats that would otherwise go empty. “ “Nearly every wedding has guest cancellations or venue minimums that need to be met. The flowers are arranged. The meals are paid for. The music still plays,” the site explains. “Not a Wedding Crasher helps couples thoughtfully invite verified guests to experience a celebration that would otherwise have empty chairs, creating connection, energy, and unforgettable memories along the way.” People’s initial reaction to strangers paying to attend a wedding might be, “No way, that’s too weird.” But in reality, especially if your wedding is large, you likely have people on the guest list you don’t know very well anyway. (Your distant cousin’s new boyfriend, for example.) What’s adding a couple of vetted strangers to the mix if it helps cover the cost of cancellations? View this post on Instagram Who would want to pay to go to a stranger’s wedding? If you’re asking, “Who would do this?” you’re likely not someone who would sign up for this service. But some people love weddings, love a good party, love dressing up and dancing, and are perfectly willing to help a stranger out in exchange for the fun of it all. In fact, the couple who founded the site, Jeff and Karina Besen, said the idea first came to them because they were looking for a unique date night. As a long-time married couple, they value going on dates—and what better date is there than attending a wedding? “You can’t just go to a wedding, at least not morally,” Jeff told WGN News . “So we connected a few dots…maybe there’s now a way to attend a wedding intentionally.” The Besens explained that many people who sign up as guests on their site are planning to get married themselves (and are looking for ideas for their own weddings) and work in the wedding industry (and are always working at weddings and rarely get to enjoy them as guests). Others have never been to a wedding and want to experience one, while others just love celebrating love. (Note: Stranger-guests have to be verified by the site, and couples have to manually approve them before they can attend, so there are some guardrails in place to weed out potential weirdos.) Are couples really using the site to fill seats? As of this writing, 24 upcoming weddings were listed on notaweddingcrasher.com . Prices range from $25 to $150 per seat, and each listing includes details about the wedding, dress code, meal, music, and other information. Exact locations aren’t listed, only the city where the wedding will take place. The couple sends pertinent details to guests after verification and approval. Some couples who’ve used the service have shared that having strangers at the wedding brought in fun energy. As one bride wrote , having a stranger-guest “amped up the vibe” of the event. Imagine folks who love to dance rolling in and getting the party started on the dance floor. It could change the whole atmosphere in minutes. It’s definitely not everyone’s cup of tea. But for those who love a wedding and don’t mind “crashing” one, it can be a total win-win for them and the couple who “invites” them. You can check out the current wedding spots available here. The post ‘Not a Wedding Crasher’ website lets people pay to attend strangers’ weddings. It’s kinda brilliant. appeared first on Upworthy .

Όπως λέει η ιστορία, τα χαρτόνια, πλαστικά τυλιγμένα δοχεία στο κατάστρωμα του t…
items.descriptionOriginal: In 1992, a storm caused a cargo ship containing 28,800 rubber ducks and other children’s bath toys heading from China to the U.S. to tumble into the North Pacific. Their unexpected odyssey became one of history ’s most unusual and large-scale ocean studies ever recorded. As the story goes , the cardboard, plastic-wrapped containers on the deck of the Ever Laurel ship had already degraded from saltwater exposure. When the storm violently tossed the ship around, at least one container broke open, spilling a colorful menagerie of yellow ducks, red beavers, green frogs, and blue turtles, collectively known as Friendly Floatees , into the ocean. Toys turned trackers These toys were designed without holes, letting them float on the currents until they reached dry land. Within ten months, beachcombers in Alaska spotted the first wave of duckies. When Seattle-based oceanographers Curtis Ebbesmeyer and Jim Ingraham, who specialize in sea currents, began hearing reports about the sightings, they knew the toys had presented a unique opportunity. Ocean currents aren’t easy to track. At the time, one common method was to release up to a thousand message-containing bottles and hope some would eventually be recovered. Only about 2% typically were. Curtis Ebbesmeyer. Photo credit: Wikipedia No scientist could ethically drop upwards of 29K plastic vessels into the ocean. But since the accident had already happened, Ebbesmeyer and Ingraham decided to make the most of the data it provided. They began using the wayward Floatees as moving data points to track the accuracy of their current computer model. They even offered $100 to anyone who reported a rubber ducky sighting. The sightings soon revealed just how far ocean currents could carry something floating on the surface Route taken by the Friendly Floatees, initially lost in the Pacific Ocean in 1992. Photo credit: Wikipedia By 1996, duckies had washed up along shores in parts of Indonesia, Australia, New Zealand, and South America. Others drifted north through the Bering Strait. They eventually became trapped in Arctic sea ice, moving roughly a mile per day across the polar cap. Years later, some of those frozen toys thawed and continued their journey into the North Atlantic. Some even floated past the site of the Titanic wreck. Although sightings have become increasingly rare, Floatees still occasionally turn up on beaches…and sell online for $1000. But these Floatees didn’t just give scientists a clearer picture of how the ocean currents move. They offered a real-world glimpse into what happens to non-biodegradable waste once it enters the marine environment. A strange lesson about plastic pollution In his book Moby-Duck: The True Story of 28,800 Bath Toys Lost at Sea and of the Beachcombers, Oceanographers, Environmentalists and Fools, Including the Author, Who Went in Search of Them , Donovan Hohn further detailed the ducks’ “incredible journey.” Cover of ‘Moby Duck’ Photo credit: Wikipedia Along the way, he learned more about the places plastic waste can accumulate and how widely it can spread. “When I first heard the phrase ‘garbage patch,’ I imagined something dense,” he told NPR. “I initially imagined it as a floating junkyard, and you’d have to poke your way through it with a paddle if you’re in a kayak. But it’s not like that. You can’t take a picture of it because that doesn’t exist. What does exist is a whole lot of plastic out there, but it’s spread out over millions of miles of ocean. And some of it floats on the surface where you can find it. And some of it floats just below the surface. And eventually all of it will photodegrade, so much of it is so small you’re not going to be able to see it with the naked eye.” In the end, an epic environmental disaster became an unexpected tool for better understanding the environment. Not bad for a toy whose greatest previous ambition was to provide entertainment during bubble baths. The post In the ’90s, 28,000 rubber ducks fell into the ocean. Scientists mapped their incredible global journey. appeared first on Upworthy .
